big_idea: The single biggest predictor of whether someone will be a great team player isn't skill or experience, it's whether they possess three virtues simultaneously: humble, hungry, and smart; missing even one creates a specific, predictable kind of team dysfunction.

tool.label: The Humble/Hungry/Smart Virtue Model
tool.text: Lencioni defines each virtue precisely: Humble means valuing team success over personal credit and readily admitting mistakes; Hungry means self-motivated, always looking for more responsibility and work, without needing to be pushed; Smart means people-smart, common sense about group dynamics and the impact of one's words and actions, not IQ. The model is used in hiring interviews, peer assessments, and coaching conversations to diagnose which virtue a person is missing and target development there.
tool.note: Smart is frequently misread as intelligence; Lencioni is explicit that it refers only to interpersonal and emotional awareness.

ideas.title: The three virtues, defined precisely
ideas.text: Humble, hungry, and smart are given specific, narrow definitions in the book so they can be assessed rather than treated as vague compliments.

ideas.title: Humble + Hungry, not Smart: Accidental Mess Maker
ideas.text: Well-intentioned and hardworking, but their lack of interpersonal awareness unintentionally creates friction and hurt feelings.

ideas.title: Humble + Smart, not Hungry: Lovable Slacker
ideas.text: Pleasant and self-aware, but does only the minimum required and frustrates teammates who pick up the slack.

ideas.title: Hungry + Smart, not Humble: Skillful Politician
ideas.text: Charming and driven, but uses interpersonal savvy to manipulate situations for personal gain rather than team benefit.

ideas.title: Virtues over skill in hiring
ideas.text: Organizations should screen for these three virtues before technical skill, since skills are easier to teach than virtues are to instill.

ideas.title: Self-assessment as culture tool
ideas.text: Introducing the model to an intact team and letting members self-identify their own gaps builds shared language for coaching without formal HR processes.

try_it: Before your next interview, write two behavioral questions that specifically probe humility.
Identify which of the three virtues is your own weakest and ask one trusted colleague for an honest example of when it showed.
In your next 1:1, describe the three-virtue model to a direct report and ask them to self-rate, then compare notes.
Watch for Skillful Politician behavior on your team this week, someone charming and hardworking who quietly routes credit or blame to serve themselves.
best_for: Team leads coaching an underperforming teammate whose problem isn't skill
less_useful: Like Lencioni's other books this is a fable first, framework second, so readers wanting data-backed rigor may want a denser source
The three-virtue labels can be used unfairly to permanently type-cast a colleague rather than as a coaching starting point
